entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Solomon is the authority on Israelite wisdom (see 1 Kings 3:1–28; 1 Kings 4:32). Many proverbs are attributed to Solomon, but he did not write all of them (see Proverbs 22:17; Proverbs 24:23; Proverbs 25:1; Proverbs 30:1; Proverbs 31:1).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Wisdom is practical knowledge that involves ethical choices. Words like right, just, and fair are associated with biblical wisdom. Gaining wisdom requires discipline, which means actively and intentionally training yourself toward wisdom and away from foolishness. The book of Proverbs encourages us to resist our natural sinful tendencies toward wrong behavior.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: This introduction explains the book's purpose and identifies the different audiences it addresses.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Simple people are like empty containers. Wisdom and foolishness compete to fill their minds and hearts (see Proverbs 9:1–18).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Proverbs help wise people understand riddles. Here the Hebrew word (khidoth) means enigmas or paradoxes—difficult sayings that need interpretation (see Judges 14:14).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Fear of the Lord means relying completely on God for everything, including knowledge and wisdom (Proverbs 9:10). It is not just a way of thinking; it involves serving, loving, and obeying God’s laws (see Deuteronomy 10:12–13). Fear of the Lord is the basis of all knowledge. How can we understand life without knowing its most basic truth—that God created it?

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content:
In the book of Proverbs, there are two paths (Proverbs 1:15):

• A wise and just path

• A foolish and evil path

The parents represent the wise path and encourage their child to follow it.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: my son: Like other wisdom literature from the ancient Near East, much of Proverbs 1–9 contains a father's (and sometimes a mother's) advice to a son. Since the son is learning his father's job, much of the teaching is about the son's future work. Some translations (like The New Living Translation) often use the term child because the lessons apply to both sons and daughters.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: garland of grace… pendant: Ornaments often symbolize wisdom and its rewards (see also Proverbs 3:22; Proverbs 4:9). This imagery encourages people to seek wisdom with effort.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: The father warns his child not to join a group of wrongdoers planning to attack innocent people. Their evil actions will eventually harm them (see Proverbs 28:10; Psalms 9:15; Psalms 35:8). The evil path involves violence and theft.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: like Sheol: In the Old Testament, Sheol is the place of the dead. It is not always associated with punishment.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Birds avoid obvious traps, but greedy people do not. When they choose violence and robbery, they risk losing their lives violently. They might die during the crime or be punished with death if caught. Even if wrongdoers succeed until they die, they will experience judgment after death, while the righteous will be with God (see Psalm 1).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: The author describes wisdom as a woman. In Hebrew, the word for wisdom, khokmah, is grammatically feminine. The author encourages his son to embrace wisdom (see Proverbs 3:18; Proverbs 8:1–9:6).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content:
Proverbs uses three main words to describe those who lack God's wisdom: 

• Simple ones (Hebrew pethim) have not rejected God's wisdom and are most open to correction (see Proverbs 1:4).

• Fools (Hebrew kesilim) have heard God's wisdom but resist it.

• Scoffers (Hebrew latsonim) not only resist wisdom but also ridicule it.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Wisdom invites all three groups to come so she can make them wise (Proverbs 1:22). Having a close relationship with Wisdom means beginning a close relationship with God, which is the basis of true knowledge (Proverbs 1:7; see Job 28).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content:
you neglected all my counsel: This is like ignoring God's call (see Psalm 14). God calls us through: 

• creation (Psalm 8; Romans 1:18–20) 

• Scripture (2 Timothy 3:16–17; 2 Peter 1:20–21)

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: I will not answer: If someone has not sought wisdom before trouble comes, it is often too late to learn.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: they hated knowledge: Proverbs uses strong language. You either love and accept Wisdom or hate and reject her.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: People who do wrong will face the results of their actions (see Proverbs 1:15–19). God will make sure that sinners get the proper punishment (see Matthew 25:44–46; Hebrews 10:29; 2 Peter 2:9).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Wise people do not fear. They trust that God is in control, and wisdom helps them deal with every situation.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: hide my commandments: This means to pay attention to them and follow them. They allow us to fully enjoy and experience life.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: The father advises his son to seek wisdom. It will protect him from bad people and the risks of unfaithful women. The son should pursue wisdom, knowing it is a gift from God.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: wisdom...understanding...insight: These three words are skills needed to handle life's challenges.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: People search for silver or hidden treasures with urgency, excitement, and hope for a reward (see Matthew 13:44; Luke 15:8–10).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: The search for true wisdom leads to God. You cannot have wisdom without the fear of the Lord (having a great reverence, honor, and respect for God) (Proverbs 1:7).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: The Lord gives wisdom to those who learn it from the Scriptures, which are his words (2 Timothy 3:16; 2 Peter 1:20–21). You cannot become wise through observation alone.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Here, common sense is the natural understanding gained by listening to God's words and observing his world. God acts as a shield, guarding and protecting those who have a relationship with him.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content:
• Wisdom will enter your heart and become a key part of your life. Instead of sometimes doing wise things, a wise person always makes wise choices.

• Knowledge brings joy because it helps people live well.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content:
• Wisdom knows when people alter words to make wrong things seem right. The right path leads to life, while the wrong path leads to death (Proverbs 1:10–19; Proverbs 2:18–19; Proverbs 5:5–6; Proverbs 9:1–6, Proverbs 9:13–18). 

• ways of darkness: In the New Testament, darkness represents evil, while light represents God's goodness (Matthew 4:16; Matthew 5:14–16; John 1:14; Romans 2:19).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Wisdom helps a young man avoid an immoral woman, enabling him to resist her flattering and seductive words. Wisdom involves emotional maturity, self-control, and understanding the intent behind someone's words.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: An immoral woman has left her husband to pursue another man. Her marriage vows before God included promises of faithfulness (see Malachi 2:14–16).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: sinks...to the departed spirits: Adultery breaks a key promise to one's spouse and to God (see also Genesis 39:2–9; Malachi 2:14).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Those who make wise choices will live in the land; those who do not will be evicted. God gave the land of Israel to his people, but they could only stay if they followed God's commands (Deuteronomy 28:9–11, Deuteronomy 28:64–68). Because they broke his law, they were expelled in 586 BC (see 2 Kings 25:1–30; 2 Chronicles 36:15–21).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Storing God's commands in your heart means more than memorizing them. It involves making them a key part of your life and acting on them.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: The Lord blesses people who trust him and seek his guidance. His correction helps those who follow him.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: People who follow God's laws often live longer. Wickedness usually harms both body and mind. However, sometimes evil people live longer than good people (Ecclesiastes 7:15–18).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content:
• Loyalty and kindness show God's deep and complete commitment to his covenant with his people (see Deuteronomy 6:8–9). 

• write them: For a similar command, see Proverbs 7:3.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: On the journey to wisdom, God guides us through the wisdom in his word.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Healing and strength mean enjoying physical energy as God's reward for following the path of wisdom.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: God receives honor and blesses his people when they acknowledge him as the source of all they have. He blesses them when they give him the best part of everything they produce (Genesis 4:3–5; Genesis 18:6; Numbers 18:12, Numbers 18:29).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: The Lord’s discipline can include hardships, disappointments, and frustrations (see Hebrews 12:4–6). Like a good father, God aims to make us wise, good, and happy.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Wisdom and understanding help you live well and solve life's problems.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Wisdom is more valuable than precious metals and jewels. It leads to a relationship with God, who gives ultimate joy (see Proverbs 2:1–8).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: The tree of life refers to the first tree in the Garden of Eden (Genesis 2:9).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: God's wisdom brought harmony to the universe. Being wise means living according to the principles found in creation.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: This passage lists the benefits of common sense and discernment, which come from wisdom.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: A wise person is a kind and helpful neighbor. Proverbs strongly emphasizes helping those in financial need (Proverbs 11:24; Proverbs 28:27; Proverbs 29:7, Proverbs 29:14).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Since we often interact with our neighbors, we should not exploit them.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: While we cannot avoid all conflict, we should not start fights.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Those who use violence will eventually face punishment for their actions (Proverbs 1:18–32), even if they appear successful in the world (Proverbs 11:16). The wise will not envy them, as they are disliked by the Lord. God's friendship offers much more than anything the violent can gain.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content:
• Discourses in Proverbs 1–9 often start with a call to listen (compare Proverbs 1:8, Proverbs 1:23; Proverbs 2:1; Proverbs 4:20–21; Proverbs 5:1–2; Proverbs 6:20–23; Proverbs 7:1–3).

• Listen...to a father’s instruction: Children should listen because they have made mistakes.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Wise people handle life's challenges well because they follow good advice.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: a son to my father...the only child of my mother: In Proverbs, both parents teach wisdom. This joint involvement is unique in ancient Near Eastern traditions.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: my commands: The words that describe a father's teaching are also used in Scripture for God's law. Fathers represent God to their children. Wise fathers' teachings align with God's law.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: In the Old Testament, forgetting means more than just not remembering; it also means failing to obey.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: she: In Proverbs, the text sometimes describes wisdom as a woman (see Proverbs 1:20–33; Proverbs 8:1–9:6).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Wisdom often leads to better relationships and more wealth, but not always.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: A lovely wreath and a beautiful crown symbolize the rewards of wisdom (see also Proverbs 1:9 and Proverbs 3:22).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Not every wise person lives longer than every evil person. However, obedience and wise living increase the chances of a long, good life (see also Proverbs 5:1–14, Proverbs 5:21–23; Proverbs 23:29–35; compare Ecclesiastes 2:12217).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content:
The father offers his children two choices: 

• Avoid evil to escape its bad effects

• Choose good for its blessings

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content:
• Wisdom's paths are straightforward (honest), while a fool's paths are dishonest (Proverbs 2:15). 

• When you walk...run: the wise achieve their goals faster and more efficiently.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: The wicked stay up at night to plan evil deeds (Psalm 36:4; Micah 2:1).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: To eat wickedness and drink violence means these traits are central to someone's life. Just as we eat and drink to live, evil people sustain themselves by doing evil acts.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Light symbolizes wisdom and righteousness, while darkness represents foolishness and wickedness (see Ecclesiastes 2:12–14). Light reveals actions; darkness conceals them. Righteous people have nothing to hide, but the wicked try to hide their actions and stumble over obstacles in the dark (see Matthew 4:16; Matthew 5:14–16; John 1:14; Romans 2:19).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: pay attention: See also Proverbs 1:8, Proverbs 1:23; Proverbs 2:1; Proverbs 5:1–2; Proverbs 7:1–3; Proverbs 8:1. The child should let these teachings change his personality, symbolized by his heart. Following wisdom for life needs a change of heart.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Wise people walk through life looking straight ahead.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Following a father's wise instructions leads to life and healing (see Proverbs 4:10).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: In the Old Testament, the heart symbolizes the center of emotions, thoughts, and reasoning (for example, Genesis 6:5; Deuteronomy 4:29; Psalm 131:1). The heart plays a key role in the struggle between wisdom and foolishness, and between righteousness and evil (see Matthew 5:8; Matthew 13:15; John 12:40; Romans 6:17).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Proverbs teaches a lot about speech because words come from the heart. One basic lesson is to avoid bad speech, which includes lies, slander, gossip, and rumors (Proverbs 6:12; Proverbs 17:4; Proverbs 18:8).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Following instructions helps you make good choices. This is especially important when dealing with a woman who behaves immorally.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: These instructions on loving one's wife and avoiding immoral women were originally for young men starting their careers (see also Proverbs 2:16–22; Proverbs 7:1–27). This topic is also common in ancient Egyptian wisdom writings.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: The lips of an immoral woman may seem sweet and tempting, but they are actually bitter and dangerous. Sexual activity often starts with a kiss, and flattering words can lure someone in.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: A relationship with an immoral woman leads to death, just like a relationship with the woman named Folly (see Proverbs 9:13–18).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: An illicit relationship may seem tempting, but it eventually causes shame. If the woman is a prostitute, the young man will have to pay her, losing income. If the woman is another man's wife, he might have to pay her husband (see Leviticus 20:10).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: People in the ancient Near East were familiar with some sexually transmitted diseases. Leviticus 15:1–15 likely describes gonorrhea. Other Mesopotamian texts mention “the disease of intercourse” and the “disease of Ishtar” (goddess of love), which show symptoms of venereal diseases.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: To drink from one's own well (see also Song 4:12, Song of Solomon 4:15) means to enjoy sexual relations within marriage. Instead of spending sexual energy on immoral women, a man should build a healthy sexual relationship with his wife. Sex should not be shared with strangers. This honors marriage (Genesis 2:22–25) and follows the seventh commandment (Exodus 20:14 and Deuteronomy 5:18).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: fawn: Compare with Song of Solomon 4:5.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Even if a man hides an illicit relationship from his family and society, the Lord knows. Adultery is a sin against God (Genesis 39:8–9).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Habitual sins are like ropes that trap and hold people.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: He dies: Young men must practice self-control, as acting on forbidden sexual desires can lead to death.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: To secure someone else's debt means to use your own possessions as a guarantee. Whether you do this to gain a friend's goodwill or to profit from a stranger (see Exodus 22:25; Leviticus 25:36–37; Deuteronomy 23:19–20), the risk is too high. It could lead to financial ruin. This warning is repeated in Proverbs 11:15; Proverbs 17:18; Proverbs 20:16; Proverbs 22:26; Proverbs 27:13.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: free yourself: The risk of disaster is so high that escaping is a matter of life and death, like animals trapped.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content:
• Lazy people sleep instead of preparing for what they need (see also Proverbs 24:33–34). They are the opposite of self-motivated and hardworking ants.

• Extra sleep and more slumber sarcastically describe a lazy person’s ambition.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Laziness leads to poverty. It will arrive quickly and harshly, like when a robber or bandit attacks and steals. See parallel passage Proverbs 24:33–34.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Eyes...feet...fingers...heart: These body parts describe a person's overall character, not just a single foolish act.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Winking...speaking...pointing: These were signals used to deceive innocent people.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Even if bad people seem to succeed, they will face sudden punishment.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: The first line shows a number, and the second line increases it by one. This method, called number parallelism, introduces a list of items. It often highlights the most important final item (see also Proverbs 30:15–23).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: A false witness distorts the truth in court or in daily conversation.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: This passage highlights the serious danger of having a relationship with another man's wife (see also Proverbs 1:8, Proverbs 1:23; Proverbs 2:16–22; Proverbs 5:1–23; Proverbs 7:1–27).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: The immoral woman uses flattering words and physical beauty to attract young men.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Sleeping with a prostitute has consequences, and sleeping with another man's wife can be dangerous. Her husband may seek revenge (Proverbs 6:34–35), and God observes and judges.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: walk on hot coals: Yes, this will cause his feet to blister. The results are terrible.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Sevenfold likely means "a large amount" because the law did not require such high repayment (see Exodus 22:1, Exodus 22:4, Exodus 22:9).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: A thief might face severe punishment, even if he had a reason for his actions. However, his punishment is less severe than that of an adulterer, who has no excuse for his crime. A jealous husband will demand the maximum punishment allowed by law, which is death (Deuteronomy 22:22).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: This is the final section in Proverbs 1–9 that warns about the dangers of promiscuous women (see also Proverbs 2:16–22; Proverbs 5:1–23; Proverbs 6:20–35).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: guard my teachings as the apple of your eye: Or, with great care.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content:
• The Old Testament uses the phrase "tie them to your fingers" as a reminder to remember important things, especially God's commands (Deuteronomy 6:8; Deuteronomy 11:18). 

• The New Living Translation's "write them deep within your heart" reflects the Hebrew saying write them on the tablet of your heart (see also Proverbs 3:3). Only obedience that comes from the heart will endure.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: In Hebrew, sister is a term of endearment that shows closeness (see Song of Solomon 4:9–10).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Wisdom leaves no room for a woman who uses flattery to appeal to a young man's vanity.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Young men who are inexperienced and not set in their ways are open to learning. Each foolish act brings them closer to becoming fools.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: The young man's father shares a story to explain his lesson about women with questionable morals.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Foolish actions are often associated with darkness (see Proverbs 4:18–19; Ecclesiastes 2:13–14).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: The woman, dressed attractively, appears nice on the outside but has many problems inside.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Prostitutes often sought customers in public places like markets and on busy street corners (for example, Genesis 38:13–16).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: The immoral woman follows religious rituals to appear good, but her actions show a corrupt heart.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: She focuses on her bed and exotic perfumes like myrrh, aloes, and cinnamon, which have clear sexual implications (see Song of Solomon 4:13û14).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: let us take our fill of love: see Song of Solomon 5:1.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: The young man's unwise actions could endanger his life (see Proverbs 5:11; Proverbs 6:32–35).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: The father emphasizes thr lesson: An adulteress may seem attractive, and a relationship with her is tempting, but it will lead to harm or even death.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Wisdom speaks openly and publicly, inviting everyone to accept her gift of wisdom. Like a prophet, she wants everyone to listen to her words.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content:
The first part of Proverbs reaches a peak when the son meets two women. Both invite the young man, and the reader, into a close relationship. The young man and the reader must choose between: 

• The woman named Wisdom, who represents God's true wisdom (Proverbs 8:1–9:6)

• The woman named Folly (Proverbs 9:13–18), who represents worldly wisdom (1 Corinthians 1:18–2:16)

Both women's houses are on "the heights of the city" (Proverbs 9:3, Proverbs 9:14), which suggests ancient temples. The choice is between the true God and false gods.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: The hilltop and crossroads are easy for everyone to reach.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: In ancient Near Eastern cities, the city gates had chambers for legal proceedings and business deals. It was a good place for Wisdom to reach many people.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Wisdom is linked to truth, understanding, and knowledge, which are correct, wholesome, simple, and clear. Wisdom dislikes deception, which is sneaky and dishonest (compare Proverbs 1:2–7; Proverbs 6:16–19).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: receive...rather: You must decide between pursuing money or valuables and seeking wisdom, which is much more valuable.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Only those with wisdom can have good judgment, knowledge, and discernment.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: People who choose wisdom, meaning those who respect the Lord (see Proverbs 1:7; Proverbs 9:10), will speak truthfully and kindly.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: The best rulers use wisdom to guide them (for example, 1 Kings 3:16–28).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: created me as His first course, before His works of old...From everlasting I was established: God's wisdom has always been. Here, wisdom is shown as a person, but it is not an actual person. Wisdom is part of God's character and nature. Unlike pagan gods, God does not need an outside advisor (see Isaiah 40:13–14). Jesus is the highest point of God's wisdom (see Colossians 1:15–17; Colossians 2:3).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: God used his wisdom to create the world. Wisdom helps us understand how the world works and shows God's greatness.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: craftsman: God's wisdom shaped creation, bringing order from chaos.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Wisdom gives great rewards to those who listen and follow it.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Life is the greatest reward for the wise. Rejecting wisdom leads to death. These verses refer to eternal life and death (see Luke 23:43; 1 Corinthians 15:1 Corinthians 15).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: The number seven symbolizes greatness or completeness. Thus, the seven columns represent the greatness of Wisdom's house, where it resides.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: In Proverbs 9:13–18, a competing invitation challenges this offer to join Wisdom for a lavish meal.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: In the ancient Near East, people held a great banquet for a marriage, a military victory, or a treaty. Wisdom's celebration marks the start of a committed relationship with the listener.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: In the ancient Near East, people built temples on high places above the city. Being wise means being dedicated to the Lord (see Proverbs 9:14 for comparison).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Wisdom appeals mainly to those who are naive and lack good judgment because they have not yet chosen between wisdom and foolishness. See Proverbs 9:16, where Foolishness copies and then distorts Wisdom's words.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Wisdom helps people handle life well.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: These verses create a break between the invitations of Wisdom and Folly. The purpose might be to warn the simple (Proverbs 9:4) that inviting mockers and the wicked is often pointless. These people have already chosen their path and respond to Wisdom's advice with violence. In contrast, the wise appreciate and benefit from corrective advice.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: fear of the LORD: Refer to study note on Proverbs 1:7.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: The woman named Folly is loud: Fools speak loudly and shamelessly but say nothing smart.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: The woman named Folly invites those who are naive and lack good judgment to join her banquet. Her invitation and advice oppose Wisdom's (Proverbs 9:1–6).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Traditionally, people built temples on the hills above the city. Folly represents false gods and goddesses who try to win the love and loyalty of God's people (compare Proverbs 9:2–3).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Just like Wisdom, Folly has prepared a banquet for her guests (see Proverbs 9:2–5). However, this meal is deceitful and immoral.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Folly's dinner guests end up in the grave, unlike the reward for Wisdom's guests (see Proverbs 9:6).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Godly parents feel joy or grief based on how well their child follows wise principles.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content:
This section is called The Proverbs of Solomon. It mostly contains short pieces of advice and observations. These sayings often use antithetical parallelism to compare wisdom and righteousness with foolishness and wickedness. The proverbs seem to be arranged randomly, similar to Egyptian and Mesopotamian wisdom literature. Some proverbs repeat: 

• Proverbs 6:10–11 and Proverbs 24:33–34

• Proverbs 14:12 and Proverbs 16:25

• Proverbs 18:8 and Proverbs 26:22

• Proverbs 19:24 and Proverbs 26:15

• Proverbs 20:16 and Proverbs 27:13

• Proverbs 21:9 and Proverbs 25:24

• Proverbs 22:3 and Proverbs 27:12

Sometimes, a group of proverbs shares a similar theme (for example, Proverbs 16:1–11).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Ill-gotten treasures...righteousness: The book of Proverbs values good behavior more than money (see also Proverbs 11:18; Proverbs 13:11, Proverbs 13:22).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: This proverb can be misused if people think outward results show someone's godliness. Job's three friends, for example, wrongly thought Job must have sinned to deserve his suffering (see Job 22:6–11).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Lazy people make unwise choices, but hard workers make wise decisions (see also Proverbs 10:26; Proverbs 26:13–16).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: the name of the wicked will rot: In ancient Israel, as in today's Middle East, honor and shame were strong motivators.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Paths symbolize life (see Proverbs 1:15).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content:
• To ignore wrongdoing suggests approval of bad behavior instead of addressing it.

• foolish lips will come to ruin: The Berean Standard Bible follows the Hebrew version (the Masoretic Text). Some scholars think this wording might have been influenced by Proverbs 10:8. Instead, they follow the Greek version of the Old Testament (the Septuagint), which says, "the one who rebukes with confidence makes peace."

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Like a fountain gives water to support life, the words of good people give life to listeners. In contrast, the hidden violent intentions in the words of bad people lead to death (see also Proverbs 10:6; James 3:1–12).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: rod is for the back: People without sense harm themselves with their words. For information on physical discipline, see Proverbs 23:13–14.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: While wealth can protect against problems, it can also cause them (Proverbs 13:8) and give a false sense of security (Proverbs 18:10–11).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Wise people welcome corrections to their thoughts or actions. They see discipline as a chance to become wiser.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: People who talk too much often reveal their lack of knowledge and cause problems for themselves (see also Proverbs 10:17; Proverbs 13:3; Proverbs 17:28).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Words express what is in the heart.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: The wicked may enjoy life's material blessings, but only for a short time, unlike the godly. Jesus also explained this truth (Matthew 7:24–27).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: This saying relates to God's covenant promises to Israel (see Deuteronomy 28:1–14, Deuteronomy 28:63–68). These connections are uncommon in Proverbs.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content:
• Here, honest practices are used in business (see also Proverbs 16:11; Proverbs 20:10, Proverbs 20:23; Leviticus 19:35–37; Deut 25:13–15; Ezekiel 45:10; Hosea 12:7–8; Micah 6:11).

• Scales often had two metal bowls hanging from a crossbar. The currency unit, the shekel, comes from the verb meaning “to weigh” (see Amos 8:5–6).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Pride involves promoting oneself dishonestly, while humility means honestly recognizing one's strengths and weaknesses.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Living rightly, which comes from wisdom, is more important than wealth. There is nothing wrong with riches (Proverbs 10:15, Proverbs 10:22; Proverbs 14:24) if earned honestly (compare Proverbs 13:11; Proverbs 21:6; Proverbs 22:16).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Our actions, whether good or bad, impact the entire city (see Ecclesiastes 8:9–13).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: This view on gossip is echoed in Proverbs 20:19.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: The future of a nation depends on wise decisions.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: This message appears in Proverbs 6:1–5, Proverbs 17:18, Proverbs 20:16, Proverbs 22:26, and Proverbs 27:13.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Respect is a lasting reward for being kind, while wealth is a temporary prize for being ruthless (see also Proverbs 10:2; Proverbs 11:18).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Good behavior positively impacts the next generation.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Discretion is the skill to distinguish right from wrong, beauty from ugliness, and good taste from bad taste.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: In the short term, bad people might succeed and good people might face hardships, but the future will correct this imbalance.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Generous people who give freely to others will succeed, but those who hoard their money will lose it (see Proverbs 28:27; 2 Corinthians 9:6–9).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Money can be a blessing from God, but it is not guaranteed. Those who trust in God will thrive (see Psalm 1).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: The suggested answer is that evil people will face punishment on earth.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content:
• In other parts of Proverbs, a crown represents: 

• Wealth (Proverbs 14:24)

• Long life (Proverbs 16:31)

• Grandchildren (Proverbs 17:6)

• decay (literally rot): A disgraceful wife is a serious and life-threatening issue.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: The wicked may succeed for a short time, but they do not endure. The family of the righteous remains strong for generations.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Being sensible means thinking about the consequences before acting. A warped mind acts without thinking.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: What is real matters more than how things look.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: This proverb is repeated with a different ending in Proverbs 28:19.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Thieves can become violent at any time due to their instability. In contrast, godly people are well-grounded, and their relationships remain stable even in tough times.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Fools do not understand what wise people know: listening is the key to learning.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Staying calm helps a wise person think clearly and avoid actions that might start a fight.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: This proverb's message is also in Proverbs 14:5.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: A wise son heeds his father’s discipline: Gaining wisdom needs discipline and correction.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Controlling what you say shows wisdom (see James 3:1–12).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Things are not always what they seem.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Money can be a blessing or a curse (see Proverbs 3:9–10; Proverbs 21:6).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: extinguished: Compare Proverbs 20:20; Proverbs 24:20.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: People mainly communicated through spoken messages. An unreliable messenger delivering the wrong message could cause many problems.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: The people we spend time with influence us.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Hard work does not always lead to success (see Proverbs 10:426; Proverbs 12:11; Proverbs 13:4) because injustice exists in the world.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Punishment can help motivate learning. Discipline shows love, while not disciplining a child can show laziness (see also Proverbs 19:18; Proverbs 23:13–14; Proverbs 29:17).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Building or tearing down a home is a metaphor for making a family stronger or weaker.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content:
• The path symbolizes life and behavior (see Proverbs 2:13, Proverbs 2:20; Proverbs 3:6; Proverbs 4:11; Proverbs 6:23).

• fears the LORD: See Proverbs 1:7.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: People can use a foolish person's words against them.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: It is easy to keep a stable clean if it is empty, but a farmer without an ox cannot harvest crops.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Honest speech and lies both come from a person's character. Compare Proverbs 12:17.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Wise people admit their mistakes and sins, which leads to change and making peace. Fools try to defend themselves by mocking guilt.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: No one can completely understand another person's emotions (compare Psalm 103:14; Isaiah 63:9; Nahum 1:7; Romans 8:27). Bitterness and joy are opposites in emotions. This poetic device, called merism, refers to these extremes to cover all emotions in between.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: A house is usually more stable than a tent, but wickedness destroys and tears down, while godliness builds up (Proverbs 14:1).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: The best choice may not always appear correct at first glance (see Matthew 7:13–14). See the parallel passage in Proverbs 16:25

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: A person's appearance might not show their true feelings.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Backsliders act foolishly against what they know is good, right, and wise.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Short-tempered people do not think about the consequences before getting angry. Planners think ahead, but people dislike them for their harmful actions.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: inherit folly: A person's true nature and attitude will eventually show in their behavior.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: This proverb might advise moderation, suggesting having neither too little nor too much (Proverbs 30:7–9).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: blessed is he who shows kindness to the poor: See also Proverbs 3:27–28; Proverbs 11:24; Proverbs 28:27; Proverbs 29:7, Proverbs 29:14.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: This proverb shares a general idea. Sometimes, fools have wealth (Proverbs 10:2; Proverbs 11:18), and poverty does not always come from foolishness (compare Proverbs 13:23; Proverbs 16:8).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: A king's success is shown by the well-being and growth of the people, not by wealth or military victory.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Wise people manage their emotions and express them in the right way.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: A peaceful heart has settled its inner conflicts. Being free from jealousy is good for physical health.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content:
• Wise people help the poor (compare Proverbs 11:24–26; Proverbs 28:27; see Leviticus 19:9–10; Deuteronomy 15:11; Deuteronomy 24:10–15; Isaiah 3:14–15; Jeremiah 2:34; see also James 2:1–13). 

• taunts their Maker: See also Proverbs 17:5.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Proverbs rarely mentions life after death. Some scholars believe this verse means God gives courage to face death with dignity and calmness.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: A great nation is not defined by wealth, power, or military victories (Proverbs 14:28) but by its moral values.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Controlling emotions and matching them to the situation helps others listen without reacting.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: A wise teacher presents lessons in an engaging way. Rude behavior describes the poor teaching of a fool.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Knowing that the eyes of the Lord watch everywhere motivates wise behavior.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: To be wise, learn from your mistakes.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: God gives wealth to the righteous (Proverbs 10:22; see also Proverbs 10:15 and Proverbs 14:24). The wicked might also become wealthy, but it will cause problems instead of blessings (Proverbs 11:4, Proverbs 11:18; Proverbs 13:11; Proverbs 21:6; Proverbs 22:16).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: God examines the heart's attitude behind sacrifices and prayers (see also Proverbs 21:27; Psalm 40:6–8; Micah 6:6–8).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content:
• Sheol and Abaddon represent the fate of the dead. Sheol is where the dead reside, while Abaddon is another name for Sheol, suggesting punishment. 

• God knows all secrets (see Psalm 139:1–12).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Mockers cannot become wise because they avoid criticism (compare Proverbs 10:17; Proverbs 13:1, Proverbs 13:10).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: People's feelings influence how they present themselves (compare Proverbs 15:30).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Our preference for knowledge or trivial things shows if we are pursuing wisdom or foolishness.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Our personality shapes how we see life.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content:
• A respectful fear of the Lord calms inner turmoil and brings peace. 

• Better a little: See also Proverbs 16:8.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: This proverb highlights the value of love over wealth. A big meal, like steak, is nice, but love is more important.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Managing your anger shows wisdom (see also James 1:19–20).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: A lazy person can find many excuses, like a path blocked with briers, to avoid work (see Proverbs 10:4, Proverbs 10:26; Proverbs 12:11, Proverbs 12:14; Proverbs 13:4; Proverbs 14:4).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: A person might not consider every aspect of a problem. A wise person seeks advice from many people.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: A wise person chooses life to avoid death.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Proud people believe they can take care of themselves. Widows in the ancient Near East were the opposite—very vulnerable and without support or protection.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: The sincerity of your prayers determines if God hears them.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Our experiences, like seeing someone smile or hearing good news, can change how we feel. This, in turn, affects our demeanor (see Proverbs 15:13).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Fearing the Lord encourages humility because respecting God helps us see we are not self-sufficient.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Our plans will succeed only if God permits (see also Proverbs 16:9, Proverbs 16:33; James 4:13–16).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: God's judgment of right and wrong is what matters (see Genesis 8:21; 1 Samuel 13:14; 1 Samuel 16:6–7; Luke 16:15). This saying is almost the same in Proverbs 21:2.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: God should support our plans (Proverbs 16:1), so it is wise to ask for his help to achieve our goals (see James 4:13–16).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: The wicked will face difficulties in life and after death. God controls everything (see also Romans 9:10–24; 2 Peter 2:9).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: God dislikes proud people who do not follow the Lord's ways (Proverbs 16:3). They wrongly think they can succeed without help (Proverbs 16:1).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: God's constant love and faithfulness are key in his covenant with Israel (see Exodus 15:13; Exodus 34:6–7; Numbers 14:18–19; Deuteronomy 7:9–11).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Better a little: See also Proverbs 15:16.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Divine wisdom is guidance from a divine source that helps the king make decisions (for example, 1 Kings 3:28; see also Psalm 72:2).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: This series of sayings reflects on the king, who symbolizes God's power on Earth.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: This proverb's message appears four times in the collection (see Proverbs 11:1; Proverbs 20:10, Proverbs 20:23).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: These proverbs assume a wise and godly king (see Isaiah 9:6–7). Many of Israel’s kings loved wrongdoing and hated truth, like Ahab in 1 Kings 21:1 Kings 21.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: The king is powerful. People should avoid making him angry and try to earn his favor.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Having wisdom and good judgment can lead to wealth, but money cannot buy wisdom.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Those who resist God and rely on their own strength (Proverbs 16:5) are acting foolishly and harming themselves. Without God's help, no one has enough resources for life.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: This saying is repeated in Proverbs 14:12.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Scoundrels, troublemakers, and violent people disrupt relationships by causing harm with their actions.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: As godly people age, they become wiser, and their gray hair is like a crown (comparee Proverbs 4:9; Proverbs 12:4; Proverbs 17:6).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Patience and self-control are more valuable than using force.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: The lot is cast: These dice were not for gambling. God used them to reveal his will (Exodus 28:30; see also Joshua 14:2; 1 Samuel 10:17–27; 1 Samuel 14:40–43).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Wisdom is more important than privilege. If children act foolishly, a wise servant will become the leader of the household.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: The Lord's refining fire (see Psalm 66:10; Jeremiah 9:7; Malachi 3:2–3) removes impurities from a person's heart, leaving only what is valuable (compare Proverbs 16:2; Proverbs 21:2; Proverbs 27:21).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Lies (Proverbs 6:16–19; Proverbs 14:5, Proverbs 14:25; Proverbs 25:18), gossip (Proverbs 11:13; Proverbs 18:8), and slander (Proverbs 10:18) twist the truth to harm others.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Mocking what God created is the same as mocking God.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content:
• Only those blessed with a long life become grandparents. Continuing the family line shows God's blessing (see Genesis 12:1–3). 

• father: This proverb applies to both fathers and mothers.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: To have a good relationship, forgive others instead of focusing on their mistakes.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Wise people listen to gentle criticism and follow good advice. Even severe punishment will not change a foolish person.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Rebellion comes from the nature of evil people who resist the consequences of their actions.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: This saying warns against teaching fools. A fool stuck in foolishness may respond with anger and violence.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: release a flood: Once a quarrel starts, stopping it is hard. Avoid disputes whenever possible (see Proverbs 10:12; Proverbs 15:18; Proverbs 16:28; Proverbs 20:3; Proverbs 22:10; Proverbs 26:21).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: This message is repeated in Proverbs 6:1–5; Proverbs 11:15; Proverbs 20:16; Proverbs 22:26; Proverbs 27:13.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: gate high: Overconfidence in winning a fight encourages people to start harmful arguments.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Wisdom is not natural; you must seek it. Wise people work hard to gain wisdom, but fools cannot stay focused.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: A foolish son: This saying applies to both sons and daughters.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Words reflect a person's character, like water springs from the earth (see also Proverbs 10:20; Proverbs 12:23; Proverbs 16:23; compare James 3:10–12).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Rumors can be tempting to listen to and share, but they are harmful. See a parallel passage in Proverbs 26:22

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: In a troubled world, only the Lord can save. The rich might think their wealth is a strong defense, but money's power is limited (Proverbs 11:4; Proverbs 13:8).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Arrogance breeds pride and causes failure because it blocks change when criticized. Humility learns from others and leads to the honor of success.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: A spiritual or emotional problem, like a crushed spirit, can be more challenging than a physical illness.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: See “Bribes” Theme Note.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: It is important to listen to both sides of a disagreement. Only foolish people make quick decisions. Wise people take time to understand.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Casting the lot: Casting lots was once a valid way to seek God's will (Numbers 27:21; Joshua 18:6–10). The Lord decided how the lots would fall (Proverbs 16:33).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Life and death: Wise people speak thoughtfully (Proverbs 10:19; Proverbs 11:12; Proverbs 12:23) because they know words have consequences (Proverbs 13:3; Proverbs 14:3).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: God will punish the powerful who look down on the poor. Wise people help those in need (Proverbs 11:24; Proverbs 28:27; Proverbs 29:7, Proverbs 29:14).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Some people who call themselves "friends" are not. Wise people look past appearances. They tell real friends from fake ones by their actions in tough times.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: It is better to be honest, even if poor, because wealth from dishonesty does not last long (Proverbs 10:2) and will not protect from harm (Proverbs 11:4; see also Proverbs 15:16–17; Proverbs 16:8, Proverbs 16:16; Proverbs 17:1; Proverbs 22:1; Proverbs 28:6).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: It is dangerous to act without understanding.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Fools blame the Lord instead of admitting their mistakes and actions.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: God will ensure that liars receive punishment (see Proverbs 12:17, Proverbs 12:19; Proverbs 14:5, Proverbs 14:25; Proverbs 19:9).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: We should seek wisdom because it helps us succeed.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: The mention of a false witness (see also Proverbs 19:5) reminds us of the ninth commandment (Exodus 20:16), you shall not bear false witness.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: A lion's roar warns of danger and possible violence (compare Proverbs 20:2). Dew on the grass is calming and helps plants grow (see Proverbs 16:14–15).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: No decision is more important for a son than choosing a good wife (compare Proverbs 31:10–31). A poor choice causes pain (compare Proverbs 10:1; Proverbs 11:22; Proverbs 12:4; Proverbs 21:9, Proverbs 21:19; Proverbs 25:24; Proverbs 27:15–17). A wise man will seek the Lord's help to find an understanding wife.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Following God's commandments, the law of Moses, keeps a person safe (see Deuteronomy 28:15–68).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Gaining wisdom needs discipline for everyone, including children (see Proverbs 10:17; Proverbs 13:1, Proverbs 13:10; Proverbs 15:31–32; Proverbs 17:10). The short-term sadness from discipline is worth avoiding disaster.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: This proverb humorously highlights the foolishness of laziness (see also Proverbs 10:4–6, Proverbs 10:26; Proverbs 12:11, Proverbs 12:27; Proverbs 13:4; Proverbs 15:19; Proverbs 18:9). See the parallel passage in Proverbs 26:15.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: A mocker cannot be helped (see study notes on Proverbs 1:22; 21:11). A leader should still punish him so the simpleminded learn a lesson.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: See Exodus 20:12; Exodus 21:15, Exodus 21:17.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Too much alcohol affects a person's judgment. The Old Testament does not oppose drinking wine in moderation (Proverbs 3:10; Proverbs 9:5; Psalm 104:14–15), but it strongly opposes excessive drinking (Proverbs 21:17; Proverbs 23:29–35; Proverbs 31:4–5).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Queen Esther was willing to risk her life and make the king angry (Esther 7).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: True friends support you, even during tough times.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: The king should embody wisdom and fairness.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Wise people know their own weaknesses. Pride stops people from seeing their faults (Proverbs 6:17–18; Proverbs 11:2; Proverbs 13:10; Proverbs 15:33; Proverbs 16:18; Proverbs 18:12; see also 1 John 1:8–10).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Differing weights and unequal measures: Merchants should not cheat customers by using incorrect weights to measure grain (compare Proverbs 11:1; Proverbs 16:11; Proverbs 20:23).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: The ability to watch and learn from experience is a special gift.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Laziness often results in poverty (see Proverbs 10:4–6, Proverbs 10:26; Proverbs 12:11; Proverbs 13:4; Proverbs 14:4; Proverbs 15:19; Proverbs 18:9; Proverbs 19:15, Proverbs 19:24; Proverbs 20:4).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Sellers need to look beyond what buyers say to avoid being tricked.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content:
• A wise lender asks for security or a deposit on a loan. A stranger was an Israelite unknown to the lender, who then required security. Proverbs advises the wise to avoid borrowing entirely (see Proverbs 6:1–2). 

• This proverb's message is also found in Proverbs 6:1–5; Proverbs 11:15; Proverbs 17:18; Proverbs 22:26.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: This view on the gossip appears again in Proverbs 11:13.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: If you receive an inheritance early in life, you might spend it all before you die, leaving nothing for later.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: See also Romans 12:17–21.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: This proverb's message appears in three other proverbs (see Proverbs 11:1; Proverbs 16:11; Proverbs 20:10).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: God clearly guides our steps (see Proverbs 16:1, Proverbs 16:9, Proverbs 16:33). We do not need to understand why things happen. We should not lose hope because God is in control.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: It is important to consider the cost before making a promise to God (see Judges 11:29–40; Ecclesiastes 5:4–6).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: A king represents God on earth, so he should help good people and punish wrongdoers.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: The Lord's light reaches the human spirit, and God sees deep into people's hearts (see Proverbs 16:2).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: God's constant love and loyalty are linked to his agreement with his people (see Exodus 34:5–7; Deuteronomy 7:7–9). The king acts as God's representative on earth, so God will guard him (see 2 Samuel 7:2 Samuel 7).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: beatings cleanse the inmost parts: See Proverbs 13:24; Proverbs 22:15; Proverbs 23:13–14.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: A king was the most powerful person in an ancient nation, and it seemed he could do anything he wanted. However, God guides the king's heart.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: This proverb is almost exactly the same in Proverbs 16:2.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: God wants worship to come from a sincere heart and lead to good actions (see Psalm 40:6–8; Micah 6:6–8).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Appearance (eyes), character (heart), and actions are all important. God dislikes pride (see Proverbs 6:17–18; Proverbs 11:2; Proverbs 13:10; Proverbs 15:33; Proverbs 16:18; Proverbs 18:12).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: The path of foolishness leads to death, while the road of wisdom leads to life.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: A marriage that appears good from the outside, like in a beautiful home, is not fulfilling if it is full of arguments (see also Proverbs 21:19; Proverbs 25:24; Proverbs 27:15–17; compare Proverbs 11:22; Proverbs 12:4b). See the parallel passage in Proverbs 25:24

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Evil people do not just do bad things; they are bad. No argument will change their behavior.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: The simple-minded learn when they see a mocker punished (see Proverbs 1:22; Proverbs 19:25). The wise do not need punishment threats because they already seek wisdom.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: The Righteous One: God observes the wicked actions done in private and will punish them for their sins. Alternatively, the Righteous One could mean the wisdom of any righteous person.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: God is fair, so he rewards good people and punishes bad ones. This is why good people love justice, and bad people fear it.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: People with common sense can avoid life's dangers.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Spending on wine and luxury stops people from saving money. They choose to spend instead of save.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: The wicked will get caught in the traps they set for others (Proverbs 26:27; see also Proverbs 11:8).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Better to live in the desert: Compare Proverbs 21:9; Proverbs 25:24.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: See also to Proverbs 3:9–10, Proverbs 3:15–16; Proverbs 10:15, Proverbs 10:16, Proverbs 10:22; Proverbs 14:24.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Righteousness and unfailing love are traits linked to Israel's agreement with God (see Exodus 34:5–7; Deuteronomy 7:9–11). The agreement promised life and honor to those who followed God's law (Deuteronomy 28:1–14).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: A smart military planner can find ways to beat stronger armies. This shows that wisdom is better than just strength (compare Ecclesiastes 7:12; Ecclesiastes 9:13–18).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Mocker: See Proverbs 1:25–27 and Proverbs 9:7–9. Also, see study note on Proverbs 1:22.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Generosity is a trait of the godly, while stinginess is a trait of fools (Proverbs 29:7, Proverbs 29:14). Interestingly, the more you give, the more you receive (Proverbs 11:24).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Human wisdom is powerless against the Lord (see Proverbs 16:1, Proverbs 16:3, Proverbs 16:9, Proverbs 16:33). Similarly, military power, symbolized by the horse, is powerless without the Lord's blessing.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: A wise person will not risk their reputation for money.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Remembering that the Lord created both rich and poor helps stop the exploitation of the poor.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: The idea of being careful appears in several proverbs (Proverbs 14:8, Proverbs 14:15; Proverbs 21:29). See the parallel passage in Proverbs 27:12.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Fear of the LORD (see Proverbs 1:7; Proverbs 9:10) is closely linked with humility. A humble person understands he is not the center of the universe. Humility is more valuable than wealth (Proverbs 16:19; see also Proverbs 11:2; Proverbs 15:33; Proverbs 18:12).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Living by deceit is risky. Corrupt people never know when others will discover their treachery or when it will backfire.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: This warns against borrowing. Other proverbs advise against guaranteeing others' debts (Proverbs 6:1–2; Proverbs 20:16).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Even a bad ruler wants advisers with a pure heart, meaning they are completely loyal and speak kindly.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: This proverb reminds wise people (those with knowledge) that the Lord controls everything.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Among the many proverbs about laziness (Proverbs 10:4–6, Proverbs 10:26; Proverbs 12:11; Proverbs 13:4; Proverbs 14:4; Proverbs 15:19; Proverbs 18:9; Proverbs 19:15, Proverbs 19:24; Proverbs 20:4, Proverbs 20:13; Proverbs 21:25; Proverbs 26:13), this one is the funniest. Lazy people will invent any wild excuse to avoid working.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: An immoral woman uses flattery and seduction to lure a young man into committing a sin.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: We learn wisdom; it is not inherited or natural. Discipline is needed to turn foolishness into wisdom.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: A person advances through hard work, not by taking advantage of the poor or bribing the wealthy (compare Proverbs 22:29).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Like the prologue in the book of Proverbs (Proverbs 1:2–7) and the introductions to the individual discourses (see Proverbs 1:8–9; Proverbs 2:1–11), this section starts by encouraging listening. This wisdom goes beyond practical advice; it aims to inspire trust in the Lord.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: This section is attributed to a group known as the wise, but their identity is unknown. There is a mention of thirty sayings (Proverbs 22:20). The wisdom sayings that follow can be divided into thirty sections. These sections are similar to an Egyptian work called the Instruction of Amenemope, which is also divided into thirty chapters.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: thirty sayings: Early scribes observed that the Hebrew word for thirty was written in an unusual form (shlshwm) instead of the usual form (shlyshym). All early translations of the Old Testament, such as the Greek Septuagint, Latin Vulgate, and Syriac Peshitta, interpret it as thirty. However, some choose to translate the word as excellent sayings.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Saying 1: God protects the weak, including the poor. Those who are wealthy should be generous to the poor (Proverbs 11:24–26; Proverbs 21:13; Proverbs 22:9, Proverbs 22:16; Proverbs 28:27).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Saying 2: An angry or hot-tempered person cannot control their emotions and shows anger at the wrong times.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: This proverb's message is also found in Proverbs 6:1–5; Proverbs 11:15; Proverbs 17:18; Proverbs 20:16; Proverbs 27:13.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Saying 4: In ancient times, stones marked property boundaries. Moving these markers was a serious offense (see also Proverbs 23:10; Deuteronomy 19:14).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Saying 5: People who improve their skills and work hard will get the best jobs and work for the best employers.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Saying 6: Many proverbs advise young men in government jobs. A ruler's rich food might tempt a newcomer to overeat due to lack of self-control. But he will be at risk when full.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Saying 7: Wealth can be a blessing from God (Proverbs 3:9–10, Proverbs 3:15–16; Proverbs 10:22), but some things in life matter more.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Proverbs highly values generosity (Proverbs 11:24–26; Proverbs 21:13; Proverbs 22:9).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Saying 9: Fools do not listen to advice (compare Proverbs 9:7–12; Proverbs 10:18), so wise people do not waste their words (see Matthew 7:6).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content:
• Saying 10: Wise people avoid unfair business practices and illegitimate gains (see Proverbs 22:28), knowing that the Lord will judge wrongdoing. 

• Redeemer: The New Living Translation is likely correct in capitalizing the word Redeemer and identifying it with God, although it might refer to a human redeemer.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Saying 11: Listen carefully: Learning helps you improve (see Proverbs 10:17; Proverbs 13:1, Proverbs 13:10; Proverbs 15:24, Proverbs 15:31–32; Proverbs 17:10; Proverbs 19:24).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Saying 12: Refer to Proverbs 19:18; Proverbs 29:17.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Saying 13: A wise parent feels joy when their child is wise (see Proverbs 10:1).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Saying 14: Sometimes sinners succeed, but the wise know that fearing the Lord brings true rewards (see Proverbs 1:7).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Saying 15: Discipline is essential for a wise and balanced life. Drinking too much (drunkards, see also Proverbs 23:29–35), overeating (gluttons, see also Proverbs 23:1–3), or oversleeping (see also Proverbs 10:5; Proverbs 19:15) leads to poverty.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Saying 16: This saying encourages seeking the wisdom that both a godly father and mother offer. Unlike other ancient Near East wisdom texts, Proverbs credits wisdom to both parents (Proverbs 1:8; Proverbs 6:20).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Saying 17: Falling for a promiscuous woman is a trap, not a benefit. Proverbs often warns against sexual relations outside of marriage (see Proverbs 5; Proverbs 6:20–35; Proverbs 7:1–27).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Saying 18: This saying highlights the foolishness of someone who drinks too much alcohol (see Proverbs 20:1).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Saying 19: See Proverbs 1:8–19.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Saying 20: See Proverbs 14:11.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Saying 21: See Proverbs 21:22.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Saying 22: Leaders need to be wise (see Proverbs 8:5–6).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Saying 23: Fools separate themselves from the community because they do bad things.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Saying 24: A wise person stays calm and strong when stressed (for example, Daniel 1:8–16; Daniel 3:1–18).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Saying 25: Wise people try to stop injustice and suffering (for example, Job 29:12–17).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Saying 26: Both honey and wisdom are sweet. Wisdom enriches the soul and creates more future opportunities.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Saying 27: Godly people do not let setbacks keep them down. • Seven times symbolizes "many times."

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Saying 28: This saying introduces the teaching of Jesus to love our enemies (Matthew 5:43–48).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content:
• Saying 29: Do not envy the seeming success of the wicked (see Proverbs 24:1–2), because their success does not last. 

• extinguished: Compare Proverbs 13:9; Proverbs 20:20.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Saying 30: The king is linked to the Lord, showing his power and rule on earth (see 1 Samuel 12:1 Samuel 12; Psalm 2).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Saying 1: Wise people make fair judgments (see Proverbs 6:19; Proverbs 12:17; Proverbs 19:28; Proverbs 24:28–29; Proverbs 25:18).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: This addendum to the thirty sayings of the wise (Proverbs 22:17–24:22) includes five more sayings.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Saying 2: A true friend does not hide problems but honestly shows where you can improve. A wise person appreciates a friend's advice.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Saying 3: A wise person finds a way to earn money before spending it on themselves.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Saying 4: Do not twist the truth, even for revenge (see Proverbs 6:19; Proverbs 12:17; Proverbs 14:25; Proverbs 19:28; Proverbs 24:23–24; Proverbs 25:18).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Saying 5: Laziness and a love for sleep can lead to poverty (see Proverbs 10:4–5, Proverbs 10:26; Proverbs 12:11; Proverbs 13:4; Proverbs 15:19; Proverbs 18:9; Proverbs 19:15, Proverbs 19:24; Proverbs 20:4, Proverbs 20:13).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: This saying repeats Proverbs 6:10–11.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: During King Hezekiah's reign from 728 to 686 BC, advisers gathered these proverbs of Solomon and added them to the collection.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: This warning advises young men entering royal service that some things are beyond understanding, like the king's mysterious reasoning (for example, 2 Samuel 11:14–25; 2 Samuel 24:3).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Just as silver is useful after removing impurities, the king’s court can do justice when removing wicked people. A small amount of evil can ruin much good (Ecclesiastes 10:1).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: To meet the king, a wise person will show humility instead of pride (compare Matthew 20:20–28).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Hasty actions often lead to regret.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: See Proverbs 11:13 and Proverbs 20:19.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Timely advice and valid criticism are valuable, beautiful, and rare (see also Proverbs 15:23; Proverbs 26:7, Proverbs 26:9). We should welcome them (see Proverbs 10:17; Proverbs 13:1, Proverbs 13:10; Proverbs 15:24, Proverbs 15:31–32; Proverbs 17:10).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Snow would be a welcome relief in Israel’s hot, dry summers (compare Proverbs 26:1). Trustworthy messengers refresh their employer by helping them plan for the future.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: In Israel, rain is rare. When storm clouds appear but do not bring rain, it is like the disappointment of empty promises. Compare this to Jude’s description of false teachers (Jude 1:12).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Honey is tasty and healthy in moderation (Proverbs 24:13–14), but too much can cause vomiting. This idea applies to other life areas. For example, visiting your neighbors is good, but do not visit too often.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Lying can lead to serious consequences (see Proverbs 6:16–19; Proverbs 14:5, Proverbs 14:25).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Surprisingly, showing kindness to an enemy works better than showing anger (see Romans 12:20).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: This proverb appears again in Proverbs 21:9.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: A spring or fountain that provides fresh water gives life. When good people let the wicked control them, what was once life-giving becomes harmful.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Wise people have self-control and are not easily dominated.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: It is not right to honor fools.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Curses and blessings can truly impact people (see Genesis 27:1–41; Genesis 48:8–9, Genesis 48:15–20; Numbers 6:23–27), but a curse without cause does not work.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: A fool is like a simple animal that needs strong guidance (see Proverbs 10:13; Proverbs 14:3).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Proverbs often depend on the situation. Deciding whether to respond to foolish arguments depends on the type of fool and the situation.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: A fool might know a proverb but not use it correctly. Compare with Proverbs 26:9.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: A fool using a proverb incorrectly might cause harm. See Proverbs 26:7.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: A fool or bystander might be lazy (see Proverbs 10:4–6) or incompetent (see Proverbs 26:6–7). Employers should be cautious!

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Even when foolish actions cause serious problems, a fool continues to act foolishly (Proverbs 17:10; see also 2 Peter 2:22).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Fools have hope because they might realize their mistakes and ask for help. However, those who believe they are wise will stay ignorant.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: The slacker: See Proverbs 6:6–11; Proverbs 10:4–5; Proverbs 15:19; Proverbs 22:13.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: This proverb is the same as Proverbs 19:24.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Wise people stay out of other people's arguments (compare Proverbs 26:21).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Lies are very dangerous because they make people act on false information. Liars cannot later claim they were only joking (see Proverbs 6:16–19; Proverbs 14:5, Proverbs 14:25; Proverbs 25:18).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: A gossip and a quarrelsome person both add fuel to the fire of trouble and conflict.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: This saying is repeated in Proverbs 18:8.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: People sometimes hide bad intentions with flattery. Eventually, the true hatred of those who speak smoothly will be revealed.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: People often face the negative outcomes they plan for others (see Proverbs 1:17–19).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: We should plan (Proverbs 24:27), but our plans succeed only if God wills it (Proverbs 16:1, Proverbs 16:3, Proverbs 16:33; James 4:13–16). Only foolish people think they control the future.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: The Hebrew word for praise comes from the same root as "brag" in Proverbs 27:1. Bragging, or self-praise, is unwise.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Fools create strong resentment with their foolish words and actions.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Anger can be dangerous, but a gentle answer can calm it (Proverbs 15:1). Jealousy is more difficult to resolve (Proverbs 6:34–35).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: A rebuke can improve life by correcting harmful behavior (Proverbs 13:1; Proverbs 14:6). Hidden, unexpressed love has no value.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Wounds from a friend come from a caring correction (Proverbs 27:5). They are better than flattery (kisses) from an enemy who wants to harm, not help.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Even the best teaching (honey) will be ignored if given at the wrong time. The key to real learning is the student's willingness to learn.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: A person who leaves his family and home is more likely to find trouble than what he was looking for (for example, Luke 15:11–16).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Heartfelt advice from a close friend is very encouraging (see also Proverbs 27:6).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: During a crisis, you might need help right away. It is important to have friends nearby and neighbors who can assist.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: People often judge parents based on how their children behave in public.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: This proverb is repeated in Proverbs 22:3.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: This proverb appears again in Proverbs 20:16.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: It is important to speak appropriately for the situation (compare Proverbs 15:23).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: a contentious woman: Compare Proverbs 19:13; Proverbs 21:9, Proverbs 21:19; Proverbs 25:24.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: iron sharpens iron: Wisdom comes from interacting, often critically, with a good friend (see Proverbs 27:6, Proverbs 27:9).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: An employer values loyal workers who safeguard the employer’s interests. Smart employers offer incentives for loyalty, like letting workers enjoy the benefits of their labor (see Deuteronomy 25:4; 1 Corinthians 9:7–10; 1 Timothy 5:17–18).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content:
• Sheol and Abaddon: See study note on Proverbs 15:11. 

• People never find true satisfaction in money, power, or pleasure.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: A person who stays humble when praised shows a pure character (see Proverbs 17:3).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: A fool's character is full of foolishness.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Agricultural property can provide food and clothing for generations. These resources need constant work and care, or they will vanish like riches.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: The wicked face God's curse for breaking his covenant (see Leviticus 26:14–17, Leviticus 26:36–37).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Wise leaders rule with justice and effectiveness (Proverbs 8:15–16).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Without laws, chaos happens and bad people thrive.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Bad people try to benefit by breaking the law. Justice makes sure they are punished, while good people receive rewards.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Virtue is more valuable than material wealth. This idea is repeated with a slightly different conclusion in Proverbs 19:1.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: his father: This saying applies to both fathers and mothers.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: The law forbade charging interest on loans to needy Israelites (Exodus 22:25; Leviticus 25:36; Deuteronomy 23:19). The rich were told to lend generously to the poor (Proverbs 3:27–28; Proverbs 11:24; Proverbs 28:27; Proverbs 29:7, Proverbs 29:14).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: A person who ignores the law does not respect the Lord (Proverbs 1:7), the one who gives the law. That person's prayers are insincere, so why should God listen?

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: when the wicked rise: See also Proverbs 28:28.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Wise people admit their mistakes and wrongdoings and seek to correct them (see Psalm 32:1–5).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: An unjust ruler will not help the poor. Like a roaring lion or an attacking bear, he ruins their lives.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content:
• burdened by bloodguilt: See 1 Samuel 25:31; Romans 2:15; Romans 13:5; compare Hebrews 10:22.

• let no one support him: Murder is so serious that a fine cannot replace the death penalty (see Numbers 35:32).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: This proverb appears again with a different ending in Proverbs 12:11.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: abound with blessings: You must earn wealth ethically, or it will cause harm and not last (see Proverbs 13:11, compare Proverbs 10:2; Proverbs 11:18; Proverbs 13:22; Proverbs 21:6).

entries.title: Proverbs
