entries.content: Giving a wrong verdict because of a bribe is wrong (Proverbs 17:23; Proverbs 22:16).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Wise people want honest feedback about their mistakes so they can improve (Proverbs 10:17; Proverbs 13:1, Proverbs 13:10; Proverbs 15:24, Proverbs 15:31–32).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Children who take advantage of their parents are wrong (see Exodus 20:12).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Greedy people fight to control situations to gain wealth. Trusting the Lord helps wise people stay calm and, surprisingly, find prosperity.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Wise people listen to others' advice, while those who only trust themselves act foolishly.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: When the wicked come to power: See also Proverbs 28:12.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content:
• A man's wisdom influences his parents (Proverbs 10:1; Proverbs 15:20; Proverbs 17:21). 

• Spending money on prostitutes quickly wastes a man's wealth.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: A fair king protects the rights of others. A ruler who takes bribes uses his position for personal benefit (see also Proverbs 17:23; Proverbs 22:16; Proverbs 28:21).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Flattery is often a trick to exploit someone (Proverbs 7:21–22; Proverbs 26:23).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Wise people control their emotions and stay calm, even when stressed.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: The oppressor should treat the poor more kindly because God created both of them (see also Proverbs 3:27; Proverbs 11:24; Proverbs 28:27; Proverbs 29:7).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Wisdom is not natural; it must be learned.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Wise people follow God's law, which shows His will.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Sometimes, you may need to add clear consequences to instructions for discipline.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: See Proverbs 6:17–18; Proverbs 11:2; Proverbs 13:10; Proverbs 15:33; Proverbs 16:18–19; Proverbs 18:12; Proverbs 19:20; Proverbs 22:4.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: he receives the oath: See Leviticus 5:1.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: fear of man is a snare: See Proverbs 1:7; Luke 12:4–5.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content:
• This superscription likely refers to all of Proverbs 30. 

• Agur son of Jakeh: Besides this mention, Agur and Jakeh are not known. If “from Massa” is correct, as some translations use, then Agur was not an Israelite (the tribe of Massa is known from Assyrian texts).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Agur admits he does not know everything (compare Psalm 73:22, where the psalmist calls himself senseless). The first step toward wisdom is admitting our ignorance.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Unlike Agur's lack of knowledge and power, God's strength and wisdom are evident (compare Psalm 18:30). This is encouraging to Agur, as he knows God protects everyone who seeks Him.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content:
Agur asks God for two things: 

• Help to avoid lying (compare Proverbs 6:16–19; Proverbs 14:5, Proverbs 14:25; Proverbs 25:18; Proverbs 26:18–19)

• To not have too much or too little

Being rich (Proverbs 3:9–10, Proverbs 3:15–16; Proverbs 10:15, Proverbs 10:22) or poor (Proverbs 3:27; Proverbs 11:24; Proverbs 28:27; Proverbs 29:7, Proverbs 29:14) is not sinful, but Agur wisely wants to avoid the problems of both.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content:
These verses describe traits that wise people dislike. Fools: 

• Disrespect their parents (Proverbs 10:1; Proverbs 20:20; Exodus 20:12; Deuteronomy 5:16)

• Deceive themselves (Proverbs 8:7)

• Think they are clean when they are not (Proverbs 20:9)

• Are proud (Proverbs 6:17–18; Proverbs 11:2; Proverbs 13:10; Proverbs 15:33; Proverbs 16:18; Proverbs 18:12; Proverbs 19:20; Proverbs 29:23)

• Hurt others with their words (teeth like swords, see Proverbs 25:18)

• Harm the poor (Proverbs 3:27; Proverbs 11:24; Proverbs 28:27; Proverbs 29:7, Proverbs 29:14)

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content:
• The number parallelism (three...four) is a method to list poetic examples. This list shows powers that are never satisfied and often dangerous. See also Proverbs 30:18–19, Proverbs 30:21–23, Proverbs 30:29–31.

• The grave, representing death, never seems to have enough—people keep dying (Proverbs 27:20).

• barren womb: Women unable to have children often long for them, like Sarah before Isaac, Rebekah before Esau and Jacob, and Hannah before Samuel. 

• The thirsty desert and a fire consume everything in their path.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: People who are unkind to their parents may face a harsh fate (see Proverbs 10:1; Proverbs 19:26; Proverbs 28:24; Proverbs 29:3; Proverbs 30:11).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: The writer is amazed at how one thing affects another.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: The writer is shocked by sex outside of marriage.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content:
• This proverb lists four things that make the earth tremble because they disrupt the natural order. 

• who is filled with food: In the ancient Near East, as in many non-industrialized parts of the world today, having enough food was a sign of prosperity.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Here is another example of number parallelism: small, seemingly insignificant animals can be surprisingly powerful and resourceful.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content:
• Lemuel, like Agur, might have been from Massa (see study note on Proverbs 30:1). Lemuel’s mother teaches him to control his desires, especially for women and alcohol, so he can rule fairly. 

• Besides this passage, we know nothing about Lemuel.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: The advice to avoid wasting energy on desire for women repeats earlier warnings (Proverbs 5; Proverbs 6:20–35; Proverbs 7:1–27).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Drinking too much wine dulls the senses. A king needs to stay alert and should not drink too much alcohol.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Instead of drinking wine (Proverbs 31:4–7), the king should defend those who cannot protect themselves.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Without God's help, finding a virtuous and capable wife is impossible (Proverbs 18:22). Such a woman, like wisdom, is more precious than rubies (compare Proverbs 3:15).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: Proverbs concludes with a strong poem honoring the virtuous wife. The acrostic format makes it feel complete and helps students learn.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: The wife works to provide food and clothing for her family.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: An excellent wife participates in business activities outside her home.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: A virtuous wife is generous to the poor, which is also a trait of wise people (Proverbs 11:24–26; Proverbs 21:13; Proverbs 22:9, Proverbs 22:16, Proverbs 22:22–23; Proverbs 28:27).

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: A hardworking wife helps her husband stand out among community leaders. In ancient Israel, civic leaders met at the city gates to hold trials and make decisions.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: The noble wife shows wisdom. She stays calm when facing the unknown. She offers advice in a charming way.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: The people who know the woman best speak about her character, skills, and accomplishments.

entries.title: Proverbs
entries.content: The book ends as it started, emphasizing the importance of fearing the Lord (see Proverbs 1:7). A woman's character matters more than her physical beauty.
